paras: The killing of Embry Thompson was the shooting of a Black man by J. A. McKintosh, a farmer, near Gainesville, Texas, on a Wednesday in late August 1900. McKintosh had sworn two years earlier to kill Thompson over an alleged insult to his wife, and he shot him on sight when Thompson returned to the county. He surrendered and was released on bond at once, and the only report found told the story as a vow kept.

McKintosh farmed four miles south of Gainesville. About two years before the shooting, Thompson was accused of having "insulted the wife of Mr. McKintosh"; the report does not say what the insult was. McKintosh was said to have sworn then to kill Thompson whenever he saw him, and the report implies that Thompson had been away from the county since.

On a Wednesday shortly before August 27, which would have been August 22, Thompson came back to the county and McKintosh shot him dead "on sight." No one else is named as taking part, and the report gives no further detail of the encounter.
McKintosh surrendered after the shooting and "was immediately released on bond." No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The killing surfaced in the El Paso Daily Herald on August 27, 1900, as a short item in a column of Texas news, set between a boy's gunpowder accident and the campaign travels of former Governor Hogg. Under the headline "Took Two Years To kill," it called Thompson only "a negro," stated the alleged insult as "the offense which cost him his life," and ended that McKintosh "kept his word." The account rests entirely on the shooter's side, and no version from Thompson's family or the Black press was found.

reader.title: Killing of Embry Thompson
bases: One named white farmer shot a Black man on sight as personal revenge for an alleged insult; no mob, band, posse or officers are reported (A1).
Only one brief item in the El Paso Daily Herald's Texas column reports the killing; no second report, local paper or Black-press account was found (A1).

accounts.label: Texas news column (shooter's side)
accounts.gist: McKintosh had looked for Thompson for two years over an insult to his wife, shot him on sight when he returned, then surrendered and was bonded out.

framing.detail: The headline 'Took Two Years To kill.' and the closing 'he kept his word' present the killing as a vow fulfilled, and the alleged insult is stated as fact ('the offense which cost him his life').

record_check.dossier: Consistent: the item says 'Wednesday' in a 1900-08-27 issue, and 1900-08-22 was the preceding Wednesday; no explicit date is printed.
Not stated in the article, which names only Gainesville, Texas, and 'the county'; Cooke is an inference from the town.
Accused of having insulted McKintosh's wife two years earlier.
J. A. McKintosh, a farmer, acting alone.
Revenge for an alleged insult to McKintosh's wife; he had sworn to kill Thompson on sight.
Thompson was at large (had left and returned to the county); not in custody.

quotes: J. A. McKintosh, a farmer living four miles south of Gainesville Texas. has been looking for a negro for two years.
Wednesday the negro returned to the county, and was shot and killed on sight.
the offense which cost him his life occurred two years ago when he insulted the wife of Mr. McKintosh.
